newsitem.title: GERMANY: Row over EMU erupts within Kohl's coalition.
newsitem.headline: Row over EMU erupts within Kohl's coalition.

text.p: A simmering row about Europe's planned single currency boiled over in Germany on Wednesday with leaders in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition parties trading public accusation and insults.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber sparked the latest row when he pledged "fierce resistance" to any attempt by Kohl to soften the membership criteria for the new currency, the euro.

He said his Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavaria's ruling party and junior partners in Kohl's government, would not tolerate any country with a budget deficit above 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) being part of monetary union.
His remarks, published in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper, drew an instant rebuke from the Free Democrats (FDP), the other junior partners in Kohl's ruling alliance.

FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt accused Stoiber of "anti-euro populism" and said the Bavarian premier and another regional leader, Gerhard Schroeder, were whipping up talk of a delay to the single currency project due to begin in 1999.
"What both of them are not mentioning is the devastating effects a delay or abandonment of the common European currency would have for industry and jobs in Germany," he said.
The Maastricht Treaty laying down the conditions for economic and monetary union (EMU) stipulates that members should not have a budget deficit of more than three percent of GDP.
Senior Kohl allies have increasingly hinted that this does not have to mean exactly 3.0 percent but the CSU has insisted anything else would weaken the new currency.

The CSU's stance has already led to behind-the-scenes spats. German newspapers have reported that Kohl approached a Bavarian representative at last week's EU summit in Amsterdam and accused the party of "unusually foolish talk" about EMU.

Stoiber, widely regarded as a euro-scepetic who cloaks his opposition to Brussels by insisting the single currency should be as strong as the deutschemark, also took a swipe at Kohl's chief lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble.
Schaeuble, the parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats, said in a weekend radio interview that figures after the decimal point were "important but not decisive".

Stoiber said if the CSU were to follow Schaeuble's lead and not insist in stability, it would be committing "the biggest breach of confidence in its history". The figure of 3.0 percent was a "synonym for the culture of stability", he said.

Gerhardt accused Stoiber of hijacking the issue of Europe for the sake of party politics, saying his remarks had "little to do with economic common sense and much more to do with Bavarian elections" due next year.

Raising public doubts about European integration has been virtually a political taboo in postwar Germany. But Kohl now faces an increasingly tough fight at home to realise his cherished project of a single currency.
The arrival of France's new left-wing government has also raised fears Paris will seek to dilute the EMU criteria.
Stoiber said Bonn would have to conflict with Paris if France made use of the "classic French philosophy" that even monetary instability could be counted as a political instrument.
